articles.title: The Federal Circuit Edits Its Damages Footnote in Constellation Designs v. LG
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
The Federal Circuit today reissued its panel decision in Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc., No. 2024-1822 (Fed. Cir. Aug. 31, 2026), four months after the original April 28 opinion. But, the court did not follow the rehearing path suggested by the adjudged infringer LG, and the April panel decision stands unchanged:
What moved in the rehearing decision was just a footnote. The April opinion gave two reasons for leaving the damages award alone even though five of the nine asserted claims are headed toward a judgment of ineligibility. The first was forfeiture. The second was that Constellation's damages expert had testified that the value of the asserted patents was tied to the technology rather than to any of the particular asserted patents or claims, and that no LG witness disputed that testimony. LG's rehearing petition pointed to that testimony to argue that no apportionment ever happened. Valuing the technology instead of the asserted claims is the thing Garretson and its descendants forbid, and the panel converted that concession into the reason the award could survive the loss of five claims. LG went on to argue that its lack of rebuttal testimony was irrelevant because the damages theory was deficient on its face.
The rehearing petition asked the court to vacate the opinion and reverse the denial of judgment as a matter of law of no damages, or in the alternative to remand for damages proceedings on the surviving claims. The court did not do any of these. It simply deleted the sentence regarding "technology based damages" for patent infringement, the sentence that would have supported infringement damages not tied appropriately to the patents being infringed. The result then is that the holding stands on forfeiture and says nothing about whether a single undifferentiated royalty survives the loss of half the asserted claims.
Here is the edit, with deleted text struck through:
During oral argument, LG argued for the first time that if we determine—as we do here—that some asserted claims are patent ineligible, we should vacate the damages award. See Oral Arg. 18:03–19:34, 42:44–45:38. This argument was foreseeable and should have been raised in LG's opening brief. See, e.g., ABS Glob., Inc. v. Cytonome/ST, LLC, 984 F.3d 1017, 1027 (Fed. Cir. 2021) (collecting cases for proposition that arguments raised for the first time during oral argument are forfeited). Even so, Constellation's damages expert, Dr. Sullivan, testified that the value of Constellation's asserted patents was tied to the technology rather than any asserted patent or claim, J.A. 20280 (Trial Tr. 42:11–23) (testimony of Dr. Sullivan), and none of LG's witnesses disputed this testimony. Cf. J.A. 20333 (Trial Tr. 256:3–16) (testimony of Mr. Lewis acknowledging that the Zenith licenses were similarly tied to the technology rather than any patents or claims).

articles.title: Personal Privilege: Why Improper Venue Did Not Stop the § 101 Dismissal
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc., No. 2025-1280 (Fed. Cir. Aug. 28, 2026).
This was an odd case - particularly because the appellant (represented by Bill Ramey) decided not to appear at oral arguments. Those arguments began with a joke about how it might be embarrassing for Lance Wyatt (Fish & Richardson), who represented the successful defendants below, if he lost the appeal. He did not lose.
In a precedential opinion, the Federal Circuit that a district court which has just concluded that venue is improper may go on to dismiss the same complaint on the merits -- in this case holding the claims ineligible. Judge Prost wrote for a unanimous panel affirming E.D.Tex. Judge Jordan's dismissal on two two independent grounds: improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b), and failure to state a claim because the asserted claims of U.S. Patent No. 6,876,979 are ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
In the appeal, AML did not contest either ruling on the merits. Its entire appeal was about sequencing. AML argued that the court should have stopped when it found the case was in the wrong forum. The stakes here are big. Dismissal for lack of venue is generally without prejudice - allowing the patentee to refile the litigation in a proper forum. The 101 ruling, on the other hand, is with prejudice and likely entirely ends the litigation campaign.

articles.title: An Ordinary Word: T-Mobile v. KAIFI and What Counts as a Patent Case
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
I wrote about T-Mobile v. KAIFI back in May 2026 following oral arguments where the court spent most of the time on one question: does the Federal Circuit have jurisdiction over this appeal?
The answer, we now know, is no. Judge Chen, joined by Judges Taranto and Schall, held that a Texas breach of contract judgment that included a judgment on whether patent claims "survive" an ex parte reexamination does not arise under the patent laws. A companion nonprecedential order transfers the appeal to the Fifth Circuit.
The contract at issue was a settlement agreement. KAIFI had sued T-Mobile on its Wi-Fi calling U.S. Patent No. 6,922,728. The parties settled days before trial, with T-Mobile taking a license, making an upfront payment, and promising a second payment if "any Asserted Claim survives the EPR" that T-Mobile itself had requested. The Patent Office then confirmed seven of the eight asserted claims without amendment. T-Mobile refused to pay, filed a diversity declaratory judgment action, and lost on summary judgment before Judge Gilstrap, who held the term unambiguous: a claim survives if the reexamination certificate confirms it. Both parties asked the Federal Circuit to decide the appeal. The panel declined, finding it lacked appellate jurisdiction, and then (oddly?) spent several pages explaining what it thinks the contract means.
